question.:question/problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x - 3 \cdot y$ along the line segment from $(4,0)$ to $(-4,0).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int_C f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}s=\int_{t_a}^{t_b} f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t,
$$

where $C$ is the line segment from $(4,0)$ to $(-4,0).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=(4)\,i+(0)\,j$ and $b=(-4)\,i+(0)\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(4)\,i+(0)\,j+t[((-4)\,i+(0)\,j)-((4)\,i+(0)\,j)] \\  & =(4)\,i+(0)\,j+t((-8)\,i+(0)\,j) \\  & =(4 - 8 \cdot t)\,i+(0)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=4 - 8 \cdot t$ and $y=0$ along the segment.

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(4 - 8 \cdot t)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(0)j \\  & =(-8)\,i+(0)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t})^2+(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t})^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(-8)^2+(0)^2} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x - 3 \cdot y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1(4 - 8 \cdot t)+-3(0) \\  & =4 - 8 \cdot t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C x - 3 \cdot y\,\mathrm{d}s & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 (4 - 8 \cdot t)\cdot 8\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =8\int_0^1 (4 - 8 \cdot t)\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =8[- 4 \cdot t^{2} + 4 \cdot t]_0^1 \\  & =8((-4)+(4))-8(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $r\prime(t)$ and $\|r\prime(t)\|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r\prime(t) & =\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\,i+\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2 \cdot t)i+\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(t + 2)j \\  & =(2)\,i+(1)\,j \\ \|r\prime(t)\| & =\sqrt{(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t})^2+(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t})^2} \\  & =\sqrt{(2)^2+(1)^2} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\left(2 \cdot x + 4\right) \cdot e^{x \cdot y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2(2 \cdot t)+4)e^{(2 \cdot t)(t + 2)} \\  & =(4 \cdot t + 4)e^{2 \cdot t^{2} + 4 \cdot t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}\int_C \left(2 \cdot x + 4\right) \cdot e^{x \cdot y}\,\mathrm{d}s & =\int_0^1 f(r(t))\,\|r\prime(t)\|\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\int_0^1 ((4 \cdot t + 4)e^{2 \cdot t^{2} + 4 \cdot t})\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\mathrm{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}\int_0^1 ((4 \cdot t + 4)e^{2 \cdot t^{2} + 4 \cdot t})\,\mathrm{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2 \cdot t^{2} + 4 \cdot t,$ $\mathrm{d}u=(4 \cdot t + 4)\,\mathrm{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{5}\int_0^1 \left(4 \cdot t + 4\right) \cdot e^{2 \cdot t^{2} + 4 \cdot t}\,\mathrm{d}t & =\sqrt{5}\int_{0}^{6}e^u\,\mathrm{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{5}[e^u]_{0}^{6} \\  & =\sqrt{5}(e^{6}-e^{0}) \\  & =- \sqrt{5} \cdot \left(1 - e^{6}\right)\end{aligned}
$$
